The third moves to something that cannot be observed — the reward is confirmed — and qualifies it immediately with Insha Allah. That qualifier attaches only to the third clause, leaving the two bodily statements unconditioned.
invocations-for-breaking-the-fast-hisn-6.timing: The chapter places these words at the breaking of the fast.
invocations-for-breaking-the-fast-hisn-6.reflection: Certainty drops as the sentence proceeds. What the body can verify is stated plainly, and what it cannot is stated with a condition attached to it.

invocations-for-breaking-the-fast-hisn-6.meaning: The request rests on a stated basis, and the basis is named before the request itself: Your mercy which envelopes all things. Only afterwards does the thing being asked arrive — that You forgive me. The mercy is described by its reach rather than its degree, covering all things, and what is finally requested is a single item falling well inside that reach.
invocations-for-breaking-the-fast-hisn-6.timing: Ibn Majah records this from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr, said at the breaking of the fast.
invocations-for-breaking-the-fast-hisn-6.reflection: The description given to the mercy is far larger than what is then asked of it. One person's forgiveness is requested on grounds said to envelop everything.

invocations-for-visiting-the-sick-hisn-4.meaning: It opens by dismissing rather than requesting: never mind. What follows reinterprets the illness instead of asking for its removal — may it be a purification. The translation supplies the sickness in brackets, since the sentence itself says only it. A condition then closes the wording, if Allah wills, so even that reinterpretation is left dependent rather than asserted.
invocations-for-visiting-the-sick-hisn-4.timing: Ibn 'Abbas reported these words, said when visiting someone who is sick.
invocations-for-visiting-the-sick-hisn-4.reflection: Nothing here asks for recovery. The supplication addresses the sick person rather than Allah, and offers a way of reading the illness rather than an end to it.

invocations-for-when-the-wind-blows-hisn.meaning: Two clauses, and they are exact opposites. Good is asked for and evil is fled from, and both concern the same subject: this wind, present and particular rather than wind in general. He is addressed once at the start and is both the one asked and the one taken refuge in. Nothing further is said about what that good or evil might consist of.
invocations-for-when-the-wind-blows-hisn.timing: The chapter places these words when the wind blows.
invocations-for-when-the-wind-blows-hisn.reflection: The wind is treated as capable of either, and the supplication does not decide which it is. Both possibilities are named and neither is described any further.

invocations-for-when-you-meet-an-adversa.meaning: Two clauses, both plural, and both position Him between the speakers and the adversary. The first is spatial: we place You before them. The second is the more familiar form, taking refuge in Him from their evil. He is not asked to act in either clause — He is asked to be somewhere, and to be the place fled to. No specific harm is ever named.
invocations-for-when-you-meet-an-adversa.timing: Abu Musa Al-Ash'ari reported these words, said on meeting an adversary or a powerful ruler.
invocations-for-when-you-meet-an-adversa.reflection: Neither clause requests a defeat or any outcome. Both describe a position rather than an event, and the adversary is referred to only as them.

invocations-for-when-you-meet-an-adversa.meaning: It makes no request at all. The first clause states a sufficiency — Allah is sufficient for us — and the second praises Him in the role that sufficiency implies, as a trustee. The translation supplies He is in brackets, since the Arabic states it without a verb. Nothing is named as the thing He is sufficient against, and no adversary appears in the wording.
invocations-for-when-you-meet-an-adversa.timing: Ibn 'Abbas reported these words for the meeting with an adversary or a powerful ruler.
invocations-for-when-you-meet-an-adversa.reflection: It is said at a confrontation and never mentions the other party. What it asserts is a relationship, and the confrontation stays entirely outside the sentence.

invocations-of-the-terminal-ill-hisn-51-.meaning: Three requests in sequence, moving outward in scope. The first two concern the speaker directly — forgive me, have mercy upon me — and are made without qualification or reason attached. The third asks for something that is not about the self alone but about placement among others: unite me with the highest companions. It is the only request naming anyone besides Allah and the speaker.
invocations-of-the-terminal-ill-hisn-51-.timing: 'Aishah reported these words, gathered by the chapter as the supplication of the terminally ill.
invocations-of-the-terminal-ill-hisn-51-.reflection: The first two requests could be made at any time. Only the third belongs specifically to the end, and it asks about company rather than about recovery.

some-invocations-for-rain-hisn-63-169.meaning: Rain is asked for, and almost every word after the request narrows what kind. Three adjectives come first — helpful, wholesome, healthy. Then a contrast sharpens it further: beneficial not harmful. Finally the timing is pinned in that same contrastive form, now, not later. Twice the wording states what is wanted and then states what is not, rather than leaving the opposite unmentioned.
some-invocations-for-rain-hisn-63-169.timing: Abu Dawud records this from Jabir ibn Abdullah, said when rain is sought.
some-invocations-for-rain-hisn-63-169.reflection: The request itself is one word long and everything else qualifies it. Rain alone is not what is asked for; a particular kind, arriving at a particular time, is.

some-invocations-for-rain-hisn-63-170.meaning: The same three words, repeated three times, with the address restated before each. Nothing is added between the repetitions and nothing is named as the thing to be relieved from. The whole supplication consists of one request and its repetition, and it is plural throughout — relieve us, never relieve me.
some-invocations-for-rain-hisn-63-170.timing: Bukhari records this from Sharik, among the supplications for rain.
some-invocations-for-rain-hisn-63-170.reflection: The chapter places it with requests for rain, yet rain is never mentioned. What is asked for is relief, and what the relief is from is left entirely unstated.

supplication-after-it-rains-hisn-65-173.meaning: A single statement, and it is not addressed to Allah but spoken about Him. Rain has been received, and the sentence assigns the cause: the bounty and mercy of Allah. Two attributes are named rather than one. Nothing is requested, and the construction is passive — we have been given — so no agent appears until the final phrase arrives.
supplication-after-it-rains-hisn-65-173.timing: The chapter places these words after rain has fallen.
supplication-after-it-rains-hisn-65-173.reflection: It is said once the rain has already come, and its only work is to name where it came from. That naming is placed at the very end of the sentence.

the-travelers-invocation-at-dawn-hisn-10.meaning: Three movements, and the voice changes in each. The first calls for a witness to the praise being offered, and speaks about Allah rather than to Him. The second turns to direct address — Our Lord — and makes three requests in a row: protect us, show favour on us, deliver us from every evil. The third drops back to the third person and narrows to one speaker taking refuge from the fire.
the-travelers-invocation-at-dawn-hisn-10.timing: Muslim records this from Abu Huraira, said by a traveller at dawn.
the-travelers-invocation-at-dawn-hisn-10.reflection: It opens and closes speaking about Him and addresses Him only in the middle. The final clause is also the only one that says I rather than we.

what-a-muslim-should-say-when-he-is-prai.meaning: All three requests concern the gap between what people say and what is true. The first asks not to be held to account for what they say — the praise itself. The second asks forgiveness for what they have no knowledge of, meaning whatever the praise did not see. The third, supplied in brackets by the text, asks to be made better than they imagine. Each clause treats the praise as incomplete rather than deserved.
what-a-muslim-should-say-when-he-is-prai.timing: The chapter places these words in the moment a Muslim is praised.
what-a-muslim-should-say-when-he-is-prai.reflection: The praise is never accepted or refused. Every clause measures it against something the praisers do not know, and asks about that instead.

what-to-say-if-you-fear-people-may-harm-.meaning: One request, and the means of carrying it out is deliberately left open. Protection is asked for from them — the feared people are never described — and the manner is handed over entirely: with what You choose. The speaker names neither the danger nor the remedy, and the sentence ends as soon as that choice has been surrendered.
what-to-say-if-you-fear-people-may-harm-.timing: Suhaib reported these words, said when harm from people is feared.
what-to-say-if-you-fear-people-may-harm-.reflection: Both unknowns are left unfilled. Who they are is not stated and how the protection should come is not stated, and the second is given away deliberately.

what-to-say-if-you-see-someone-afflicted.meaning: Praise is offered and two reasons are attached to it, both comparative. The first names the affliction directly as a test, and states that the speaker was saved from it. The second widens past the person being looked at to much of His creation, and says the speaker was favoured over them. The one afflicted is addressed as you, so the comparison is spoken in their presence.
what-to-say-if-you-see-someone-afflicted.timing: Ibn Majah records this from Ibn 'Umar, said on seeing someone afflicted by misfortune.
what-to-say-if-you-see-someone-afflicted.reflection: Nothing is asked for the afflicted person. Both clauses concern the speaker's own position, and the affliction is named only as the thing that was avoided.

what-to-say-when-entering-the-home-hisn-.meaning: The same phrase opens two clauses describing opposite movements — in the name of Allah we enter, and in the name of Allah we leave. Entering and leaving are given identical wording, so neither is treated as the more significant. A third clause then leaves motion behind altogether and states where trust is placed. It is plural throughout and contains no request.
what-to-say-when-entering-the-home-hisn-.timing: Abu Dawud records this from AbuMalik Al-Ash'ari, said on entering the home.
what-to-say-when-entering-the-home-hisn-.reflection: The chapter assigns it to entering, yet the wording covers leaving in the same breath. Both directions are named before the sentence settles on trust.

what-to-say-when-leaving-the-home-hisn-1.meaning: Allah is named three times across two short sentences, and each naming does different work. The first invokes the name, the second places trust in Him, and the third denies that might or power exists anywhere apart from Him. No request appears at any point. The movement runs from invoking, to relying, to a denial that leaves nothing else to rely on.
what-to-say-when-leaving-the-home-hisn-1.timing: The chapter places these words at the moment of leaving the home.
what-to-say-when-leaving-the-home-hisn-1.reflection: The final clause supplies the reason the second is possible. Trust is placed first, and only afterwards is it explained why nothing else could have held it.

what-to-say-when-slaughtering-or-sacrifi.meaning: It opens with two declarations, the name of Allah and His greatness, before addressing Him directly. What follows is a statement of ownership made in both directions: it is from You and belongs to You. Only once that ownership is established does a request appear, and it is a single one — accept this from me. He is addressed twice, once before the statement and once before the request.
what-to-say-when-slaughtering-or-sacrifi.timing: The chapter places these words at the slaughter or sacrifice of an animal.
what-to-say-when-slaughtering-or-sacrifi.reflection: What is offered is said to come from Him and to belong to Him before anything is asked. The only request made is that it be received.

what-to-say-when-you-are-fasting-and-som.meaning: The words are not addressed to Allah at all. They are spoken to the person who has been rude, and they state a fact rather than making a request or returning an insult. The statement is then repeated once, and the repetition adds no new information — the same three words twice over. Nothing is asked for, nothing is denied, and the other person’s conduct is never described or answered directly.
what-to-say-when-you-are-fasting-and-som.timing: Recorded in the Muwatta of Malik, said while fasting when someone is rude.
what-to-say-when-you-are-fasting-and-som.reflection: It answers rudeness by naming the speaker’s own state rather than the other’s behaviour. Repetition is the only emphasis available, since no further words are ever added.

what-to-say-when-you-feel-frightened-his.meaning: It is a declaration rather than a request, and nothing in it refers to fear or to whatever is feared. The sentence is built as an exclusion: it denies the right of worship to everything, then admits a single exception. No protection is asked for, no danger is named, and the one saying it does not appear anywhere in the wording.
what-to-say-when-you-feel-frightened-his.timing: Abu Sa’id Al-Khudri reported these words, said at the moment fear is felt.
what-to-say-when-you-feel-frightened-his.reflection: The chapter assigns it to fright, yet the words never mention it. What stands in place of a request is a statement about who alone is owed worship.
